tldr: When quadrupedal robots walk on discontinuous sparse terrain such as stepping stones and gaps, conventional methods that process every cell of a terrain map suffer from explosive computational cost as resolution increases. In this paper, the authors propose DELTA, which adaptively samples and attends only to necessary locations conditioned on robot state. DELTA decouples computational cost from map resolution, speeds up training by about 10x, and achieves a 100% traversal rate on the physical robot RAIBO2 without any explicit foothold planner.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline and encoder architecture of the proposed DELTA. (a) DELTA extracts a compact terrain representation from the robot's proprioception and local elevation map, feeding it to the policy network. (b) It predicts sampling locations from proprioception, refines them using scout patches, performs adaptive patch encoding that separates center and surrounding context, and updates terrain representations through multi-head cross-attention.
overview:
For a quadrupedal robot to traverse sparse terrain with discontinuous footholds like stepping stones and gaps, it must identify where to place its feet with millimeter-level precision. Stepping even slightly off course causes an immediate fall. Recently, attention-based map encoding (AME) using reinforcement learning (RL) has drawn interest because it automatically guides attention from elevation maps to safe landing zones. However, AME extracts features across all map cells using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and treats every cell as an attention candidate. Increasing resolution to capture narrow footholds sharply raises computational cost, creating a major bottleneck for simulation training and on-robot deployment.

Inspired by Deformable DETR from object detection (which attends only around local reference points), the authors developed DELTA to replace full-map computation with adaptive sampling of promising locations conditioned on the robot's state. Proprioceptive cues like joint states and body velocities predict initial sampling positions. DELTA then inspects small local scout patches to refine these positions and processes only a fixed number of tokens. As a result, the encoder's computational cost remains completely constant, regardless of how fine the map resolution becomes.

In simulation benchmarks, DELTA matched AME's high traversal rate at standard resolution while reducing the training time to reach a 90% success rate by nearly 10x (9.9x speedup). In higher-resolution tests, it boosted traversal success on narrow stepping stones from AME's 68.0% to 95.9%. DELTA also outperformed AME by over 70 percentage points on unseen mixed obstacle courses and achieved a 100% traversal rate across seven challenging real-world courses via zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on RAIBO2 without extra fine-tuning.
contributions: Proposed DELTA, a terrain encoder with fixed computational cost independent of map resolution by adaptively placing sampling locations based on robot state
Sped up training wall-clock time by 9.9x while matching the traversal performance of baseline AME at standard resolution
Leveraged high-resolution terrain maps without adding encoder cost, achieving a 95.9% success rate on fine-grained stepping stones compared to AME's 68.0%
Dramatically improved average traversal success on unseen mixed courses from AME's 26.0% to 96.6%, and achieved 100% zero-shot traversal on the physical robot RAIBO2

sections.heading: Introduction: Why Is Spotting Footholds So Hard for Legged Robots?
sections.summary: On discontinuous terrain like stepping stones and gaps, safe landing spots are extremely limited. Conventional attention-based encoders process entire maps densely, causing computational loads to surge with resolution. DELTA resolves this by adaptively sampling only a small set of points based on state.
sections.details:
Unlike flat ground or gentle slopes, sparse terrain with isolated stepping stones or open slits leaves very few safe landing zones. Missing a foothold by just a few centimeters or catching a toe on a trench edge leads to an immediate fall, requiring highly precise foot placement.

Traditionally, model-based planners optimized foothold trajectories online using geometric and dynamic models. However, slipping during contact and unmodeled dynamics easily cause mismatches between plans and real motions, and solving for multiple future footholds simultaneously incurs heavy computation. On the other hand, end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) builds strong robustness through large-scale simulation parallelism and domain randomization. In particular, Attention-based Map Encoding (AME), which queries elevation maps with proprioceptive features, has shown great promise in discovering landing zones autonomously without explicit foothold labels.

However, existing AME has a critical bottleneck. It extracts features across every cell of the elevation map using CNNs and treats every cell as an attention key-value candidate, meaning computational cost (FLOPs) scales sharply with map resolution. While high resolution is essential for resolving narrow footholds and sharp edges, rising computation slows training down and threatens real-time inference on physical hardware.

To overcome this, the authors adapted the core idea of Deformable DETR from computer vision to terrain perception. Instead of scanning the entire map exhaustively, DELTA predicts where the robot is likely to step based on its current state, extracts small local patches around those spots, and attends only to them. This cleanly decouples encoder computational cost from terrain map resolution.

captions.F1: The physical robot RAIBO2 traversing an unseen mixed sparse terrain. Without an explicit foothold planner, it steps precisely across discontinuous footholds like stepping stones and stairs using only DELTA's state-adaptive terrain feature extraction and an RL policy.

sections.heading: Method: How DELTA Decouples Computation from Resolution
sections.summary: DELTA predicts initial sampling points from proprioception, refines them with scout patches, separately encodes center and contextual elevations, and computes multi-head attention. This aggregates rich local terrain features at a constant computational cost regardless of map resolution.
sections.details:
DELTA's overall framework and algorithm consist of three main parts: the control pipeline, the DELTA encoder architecture, and training details.

- **Overall Control Architecture**:
The robot observes proprioceptive states $p_t$ (gravity vector, base linear and angular velocities, joint positions and velocities, and previous action targets) and a robot-centric 3D local elevation map $M_t$ (height $H$ \times width $W$ \times 3 channels). The DELTA encoder $f_\theta$ processes these to output a compact $D$-dimensional terrain feature vector $e_t$. Concatenating $e_t$ with proprioception $p_t$ yields the input for the Actor (policy) and Critic (value function) MLPs, which output joint target positions executed by PD controllers.

- **Inside the DELTA Encoder**:
The encoder consists of $L$ layers that sequentially update an initial query $q_0$ constructed from proprioception. Each layer carries out four key steps:
  1. **State-Conditioned Sampling**: Predicts offsets from the current query to determine $K$ initial candidate sampling points $s^0$ per attention head.
  2. **Scout-Guided Refinement**: Because state-predicted locations might land in unsafe zones, a small scout patch ($P_s \times P_s$) is extracted around each candidate using bilinear interpolation. The scout patch evaluates local elevation profile to compute a refinement offset, nudging the point to a safer final position $s$.
  3. **Adaptive Patch Encoding**: Extracts elevation patches from the refined locations to create tokens. The final layer extracts wider $P \times P$ patches; to avoid distraction from irrelevant surrounding terrain patterns, it separates the patch into a touchdown "center region" and an external "context region," filtering surrounding context via a sigmoid gate before fusing them.
  4. **Multi-Head Cross-Attention**: Computes cross-attention from query $q_l$ across the fixed set of $N_h \times K$ generated tokens. Applying non-affine RMSNorm to the Value branch prevents tokens with small attention weights from dominating the output with excessively large vector norms.

- **Policy Learning and Curriculum**:
The policy is trained with PPO, using a reward structure based on RAIBO2 tuned for sparse terrain (e.g., penalties for prolonged ground contact and foot-edge collisions). The training environment features eight terrain types (five continuous, three discrete) across ten difficulty stages, supported by an automated curriculum that promotes or demotes stages and adaptively oversamples terrain types where the robot struggles.

sections.heading: Experiments & Results: 10x Faster Training and Agile Traversal on Unseen Courses
sections.summary: In simulation, DELTA substantially reduced FLOPs, sped up training by roughly 10x, and outperformed baselines on high-resolution fine stepping stones and unseen mixed courses. Furthermore, the physical robot RAIBO2 cleared 100% of trials across seven diverse courses.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted in the RaiSim simulator and on the physical quadruped RAIBO2. DELTA was evaluated against two baselines: "MLP" (which flattens the elevation map into an MLP) and "AME" (which applies dense cross-attention over all map cells).

- **Traversal Performance and Sample Efficiency (Simulation)**:
At standard resolution ($26 \times 16$), DELTA achieved a 96.4% success rate at the highest difficulty (Stage 10), matching AME's 96.3%. However, DELTA reached the 90% success threshold in only $2{,}210 \pm 160$ training iterations—a 75.1% reduction compared to AME. In terms of wall-clock training time, DELTA took $5.06 \pm 0.33$ hours compared to AME's roughly 50 hours, delivering a **9.9x speedup**.

- **High Resolution and Computational Cost**:
On "fine-grained stepping stones" where the stone radius was cut in half, the standard resolution grid spacing (~8 cm) was too coarse to resolve safe footholds. Increasing resolution to $41 \times 25$ (~5 cm spacing) allowed DELTA to reach a **95.9%** success rate, while AME plateaued at 68.0% within a 30,000-iteration budget. Moreover, while AME's encoder FLOPs jumped from 27.57 M to 67.91 M, DELTA's cost stayed constant at **4.496 M FLOPs** due to fixed sampling points—a 93.4% FLOP reduction at high resolution.

- **Generalization to Unseen Mixed Courses**:
On four unseen evaluation courses combining stairs, gaps, and stepping stones in sequence, AME's success rate collapsed to 26.0% (62.7% traversal rate). In contrast, DELTA maintained a **96.6% success rate (98.4% traversal rate)**. While AME was distracted by irrelevant features when past terrain, borders, and upcoming footholds mingled in the local map, DELTA's state-conditioned sampling and center-context separation effectively removed ambiguity.

- **Ablation Studies and Attention Visualization**:
Removing scout-guided refinement dropped the proportion of final sample points landing on steppable surfaces from 85.4% to 68.7%. Removing adaptive patch encoding (center-context separation) cut unseen mixed course success from 96.6% down to 56.1%, confirming its role in generalization. Attention weight analysis revealed that DELTA naturally placed **2.11x** higher attention weight on upcoming touchdown footholds relative to a uniform distribution, even without explicit foothold supervision.

- **Real-World Experiments (RAIBO2)**:
Using front and rear Intel RealSense D430 depth cameras, the system reconstructed a $41 \times 25$ elevation map in real time and executed the policy at 100 Hz on an onboard Jetson AGX Orin via TensorRT. Across seven obstacle courses—including gaps, stepping stones, and combinations with stairs—RAIBO2 achieved a **100% success rate** over 21 trials (3 runs per course), demonstrating robust real-world reliability.

Black dots represent unsampled cells; color shifts from blue to red denote higher attention. Without foothold supervision, samples naturally cluster on steppable surfaces with strong attention on imminent touchdown locations.

Gap widths ranged from 10 to 20 cm, and stepping stones were spaced 15 cm apart. RAIBO2 completed all trials using raw elevation maps with sensor noise handling, without explicit path planning.

sections.heading: Conclusion & Future Work: Expanding What Legged Robots Can Do Without Explicit Planners
sections.summary: DELTA is an efficient terrain encoder that completely decouples computation from map resolution via state-conditioned deformable sampling. It delivers high traversal capability, superior generalization, and ~10x training speedups, culminating in a 100% real-world success rate.
sections.details:
This paper introduced DELTA, a deformable elevation-based local terrain attention encoder designed for quadrupedal robots navigating sparse, discontinuous terrain.

DELTA's core strength lies in sampling and encoding only essential terrain evidence conditioned on the robot's proprioception, keeping encoder computation constant regardless of elevation map resolution. At standard resolution, it matches the performance of dense attention (AME) while slashing training time to 90% success by about 10x. By scaling gracefully to high-resolution maps, DELTA significantly outperforms baselines on fine-grained sparse terrain and unseen composite tracks. Furthermore, zero-shot transfer onto the physical RAIBO2 robot confirms that quadrupeds can overcome diverse real-world obstacles without relying on explicit foothold planners or online trajectory optimization.

For future work, the authors plan to incorporate uncertainty representations for measurement noise and extend the framework to multi-channel terrain representations that capture additional surface properties, such as friction coefficients and semantic material types.

takeaways: Shifting from dense full-map processing to state-conditioned sparse sampling over local patches fundamentally resolves the trade-off between map resolution and computational cost.
Scout-guided refinement (coarse prediction followed by local patch adjustment) autonomously guides sampling points toward steppable surfaces without foothold supervision.
Gated separation of local patch centers (contact surface) from surrounding context (edges and drops) prevents overfitting to specific terrain layouts and significantly boosts generalization.
Pruning redundant computation speeds up training, allowing the same compute budget to handle higher-resolution perception for superior precision on narrow footholds.
limitations: While the encoder computation is independent of map resolution, building the elevation map, transferring memory tensors, and preprocessing still scale with map size.
Due to hardware safety concerns, physical experiments were conducted only with high-resolution DELTA, leaving out direct real-world benchmark comparisons against baselines.
The current implementation relies solely on geometric elevation data, lacking support for deformable terrain (like tall grass) or surface property variations (like wet, low-friction floors).
